sections.title: Supplier Selection and Approval
sections.summary: Supplier quality begins before the first purchase order. Quality managers must establish systematic processes for identifying, evaluating, qualifying, and approving suppliers. The selection process must balance quality capability, cost, delivery performance, and strategic fit. Poor supplier selection is one of the most expensive quality failures because it propagates through the entire value chain.

concepts.definition: Structured assessment across four dimensions: Quality (process capability, quality system certification, defect history, corrective action responsiveness), Cost (unit price, total cost of ownership including quality costs), Delivery (on-time delivery rate, lead time, flexibility), Service (technical support, communication, responsiveness to changes). Weighted scoring matrices assign importance weights to each criterion based on the organization's strategic priorities.
concepts.formula:
Weighted Score = Σ(Criterion Weight × Criterion Rating)
Total weights must sum to 100%
Example: Quality 40% × 8 + Cost 25% × 7 + Delivery 20% × 9 + Service 15% × 6 = 7.65
concepts.examTip: Quality weighting should generally be highest. If a scenario presents a supplier with lowest price but poor quality history, the total cost of ownership (including quality failures) typically makes them the most expensive option.

concepts.definition: Systematic verification that a potential supplier can consistently meet requirements. Steps: preliminary assessment (questionnaire, financial review), capability evaluation (process audit, sample evaluation), trial production (first article inspection, PPAP), qualification decision (approved, conditionally approved, rejected), ongoing monitoring. Qualification does not end at approval — it includes periodic re-evaluation.
concepts.examTip: First Article Inspection (FAI) and Production Part Approval Process (PPAP) are critical qualification tools. FAI verifies that the supplier can produce one conforming unit; PPAP verifies they can do it consistently.

concepts.definition: Controlled registry of suppliers who have completed the qualification process and are authorized to provide specific materials, components, or services. The ASL typically includes: supplier name, approved scope (which parts/materials), qualification status (full, conditional, probationary), review dates, and performance ratings. Purchasing must be restricted to ASL suppliers for controlled items.
concepts.examTip: An ASL without purchasing enforcement is useless. The quality system must have controls ensuring that purchasing cannot bypass the ASL for critical materials.

concepts.definition: Comprehensive cost assessment that goes beyond unit purchase price to include: acquisition costs (purchasing, logistics, customs), quality costs (incoming inspection, rework, warranty attributable to supplier), inventory costs (carrying cost, safety stock due to unreliable delivery), risk costs (supply disruption, single-source dependency), and administrative costs (supplier management overhead).
concepts.formula: TCO = Purchase Price + Shipping + Inspection + Quality Failures + Inventory Carrying + Administrative + Risk Costs
concepts.examTip: A supplier with a 5% lower unit price but 3x the defect rate almost always has a higher TCO. Frame supplier quality arguments in TCO terms for maximum leadership impact.

keyFigures: Deming (cease dependence on inspection — build quality at the source)

practiceQuestions.q: A procurement manager argues for selecting Supplier A (lowest unit price, no ISO certification, 92% OTD) over Supplier B (10% higher unit price, ISO 9001 certified, 99% OTD, lower defect rate). Using TCO analysis, the quality manager should:
options: Request a full TCO comparison including quality, delivery, and risk costs
Reject Supplier A outright — no ISO certification is unacceptable
Accept Supplier A with increased incoming inspection
practiceQuestions.explanation: The unit price difference tells only part of the story. A TCO analysis would include the cost of Supplier A's 8% late deliveries (line stoppages, expediting), the cost of higher defect rates (incoming inspection, rework, potential escapes), and the risk of no formal quality system. TCO typically favors the higher-quality supplier.

flashcards.back: AIAG standard for supplier qualification in automotive (widely adopted elsewhere). 18 elements including: design records, engineering change documents, DFMEA, process flow diagram, PFMEA, control plan, MSA results, dimensional results, material test results, initial process capability study, PSW (Part Submission Warrant).

Single source: deeper relationship, volume leverage, simpler management, BUT high supply disruption risk. Dual source: risk mitigation, competitive leverage, BUT split volumes reduce leverage, more management overhead. Strategy depends on component criticality and supply market conditions.

Evaluate: financial stability (bankruptcy risk), geographic risk (natural disaster, geopolitical), capacity risk (ability to scale), quality risk (process capability, system maturity), dependency risk (percentage of their business you represent). Mitigate through dual sourcing, safety stock, contractual protections, and development programs.

sections.title: Supplier Performance Monitoring
sections.summary: Ongoing supplier performance monitoring ensures that qualified suppliers continue to meet requirements. Quality managers must establish metrics, reporting cadences, and escalation processes that provide early warning of supplier quality deterioration and enable data-driven supplier management decisions.

concepts.definition: Periodic (monthly/quarterly) performance assessment across key dimensions. Typical metrics: PPM (Parts Per Million defective), OTD (On-Time Delivery percentage), SCAR responsiveness (Supplier Corrective Action Request closure time), first-pass yield at incoming, number of customer escapes attributable to supplier. Scorecards should be shared with suppliers, reviewed jointly, and linked to business consequences (preferred status, volume allocation, development support, or probation/removal).
concepts.formula:
PPM = (Defective Parts / Total Parts Received) × 1,000,000
OTD = (On-Time Deliveries / Total Deliveries) × 100%
concepts.examTip: PPM is the standard quality metric for supplier performance. World-class target: < 50 PPM for direct materials. Scorecards without consequences are ignored.

concepts.definition: Systematic evaluation of a supplier's processes, systems, and capabilities. Types: First-party (supplier's internal audit), Second-party (customer audits the supplier), Third-party (independent certification body). Audit types by focus: System audit (QMS compliance), Process audit (specific manufacturing process — VDA 6.3 is common in automotive), Product audit (finished product conformance). Second-party audits provide the deepest insight into supplier capability for your specific requirements.
concepts.examTip: VDA 6.3 process audit methodology is widely used in automotive — know it exists and that it evaluates process capability rather than system documentation.

concepts.definition: Statistical inspection method: inspect a random sample from a lot and accept or reject the entire lot based on the number of defects found in the sample. Key parameters: AQL (Acceptable Quality Level — maximum percent defective considered satisfactory as process average), LTPD (Lot Tolerance Percent Defective — quality level that the plan should reject), α (producer's risk — probability of rejecting a good lot), β (consumer's risk — probability of accepting a bad lot). ANSI/ASQ Z1.4 (attributes) and Z1.9 (variables) are standard plans.
concepts.formula:
OC Curve: plots Probability of Acceptance vs. Actual Lot Quality
At AQL: Pa ≈ 1 − α (high probability of acceptance)
At LTPD: Pa ≈ β (low probability of acceptance)
Ideal OC curve is a step function — sample size determines discrimination
concepts.examTip: Know the relationship between sample size and discrimination: larger samples produce steeper OC curves (better discrimination between good and bad lots). AQL is NOT the acceptable defect rate — it is the process average at which the plan has high acceptance probability.

concepts.definition: Proactive programs to improve supplier capabilities rather than simply rejecting non-conforming product. Activities include: technical assistance (engineering support for process improvement), training (quality tools, lean methods), joint improvement projects (kaizen events at supplier facility), technology transfer, mentoring/coaching. Development is an investment — typically reserved for strategic suppliers with strong relationship potential but capability gaps.
concepts.examTip: The modern quality management approach favors supplier development over adversarial inspection-based relationships. Development builds long-term capability; inspection catches defects after they occur.

practiceQuestions.q: A supplier's PPM has gradually increased from 120 to 450 over six months despite two SCARs. The MOST appropriate escalation action is:
options: Issue a third SCAR with a tighter deadline
Place the supplier on probation with a 90-day improvement plan and onsite audit
Immediately disqualify the supplier and find an alternative
practiceQuestions.explanation: Two ineffective SCARs indicate a systemic supplier issue that paperwork alone cannot solve. Probation with a structured improvement plan and onsite audit provides both consequence (probation) and support (direct assessment of root causes). Immediate disqualification may be premature if no alternative is qualified; increased inspection treats the symptom, not the cause.

practiceQuestions.q: An OC curve for a sampling plan shows Pa = 0.95 at p = 1% and Pa = 0.10 at p = 5%. The AQL and LTPD are approximately:
options: Cannot be determined from this information
practiceQuestions.explanation: AQL is the quality level with high probability of acceptance (Pa = 0.95 at 1% defective → AQL ≈ 1%). LTPD is the quality level with low probability of acceptance (Pa = 0.10 at 5% defective → LTPD ≈ 5%). The OC curve visualizes the sampling plan's discriminating power between these two levels.

flashcards.back: PPM = (Defective parts / Total parts) × 1,000,000. Example: 12 defects in 50,000 parts = 240 PPM. Industry targets vary: automotive typically <50 PPM for Tier 1; electronics may target <10 PPM for critical components.

AQL (Acceptable Quality Level): process average at which sampling plan accepts lots ~95% of the time (producer's risk α ≈ 5%). LTPD (Lot Tolerance Percent Defective): quality level at which plan rejects lots ~90% of the time (consumer's risk β ≈ 10%). The gap between AQL and LTPD is the plan's 'zone of indifference.'

Formal request to a supplier to investigate a quality nonconformance, identify root cause, implement corrective action, and verify effectiveness. Should include: problem description, evidence, deadline, required response format (8D or equivalent). Track closure time and effectiveness as supplier performance metrics.

Reduced inspection frequency for suppliers with demonstrated quality performance. After a defined number of consecutive accepted lots, inspection frequency is reduced (e.g., inspect every 3rd or 5th lot). Reverts to normal inspection if a rejection occurs. Rewards good performance and reduces appraisal costs.
